name: 6-APB
addictionPotential: Moderately addictive with a high potential for abuse
toxicities: Toxicity data are very limited due to short human-use history. Repeated or high-dose 6-APB is likely to have some form of neurotoxicity and cardiotoxicity given its similarity to MDMA. Its potent 5-HT2B agonism may cause cardiotoxicity with long-term or chronic use, including valvular heart disease.
effectsSummary: 6-APB as a benzofuran empathogen and stimulant. Its pharmacology, metabolism and toxicity data are very limited; 5-HT2B agonism raises concern for cardiotoxicity with long-term or chronic use. The effects index is based on anecdotal reports.
dosageRemark: The archived oral dose table lists threshold 15 mg, light 30-60 mg, moderate 60-90 mg, strong 90-120 mg and heavy 120 mg+; total duration 7-10 h, onset 30-60 min, comeup 60-120 min, peak 3-4 h, offset 2-3 h and afterglow 6-48 h. Educational user/resource compilation, not a recommendation. The model does not represent the threshold separately, so 15 mg is preserved here and lightMin follows the source light range lower bound.
generalRisks: 6-APB has a short human-use history and toxicity data are sparse. Repeated/high-dose exposure may be neurotoxic and cardiotoxic; chronic use may cause valvular heart disease through 5-HT2B agonism.
longtermRisks: Long-term or chronic 6-APB use may be cardiotoxic and cause valvular heart disease due to significant 5-HT2B receptor affinity.
saferUse: Harm reduction is strongly recommended, given how little is known about the pharmacology, metabolism and toxicity.
It warns against repeated or high-dose use because of likely neurotoxicity and cardiotoxicity, including possible valvular disease with chronic exposure.
summary: A stimulant, empathogen and analog of MDA. Typically more visual than MDMA or MDA, as well as having a much longer onset and duration. Users often report a slightly more psychedelic headspace as well. Commonly sold as an alternative to MDMA and MDA.
